title: Calibration, Architecture, and Distribution Shift in Predictive Uncertainty Estimation
abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification matters for high-stakes tabular classification, yet the comparative influence of architecture and post-hoc calibration on uncertainty quality remains underexplored, particularly outside in-distribution conditions. We present a matched-protocol benchmark on 36 OpenML-CC18 datasets comparing three GBDTs, a single MLP, MC-Dropout, and deep ensembles of three, five, and ten members under five post-hoc calibration methods, with additional evaluation under Gaussian feature shift, symmetric label noise, split-conformal coverage, and a sub-comparison against TabPFN v2. All paired comparisons use Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm corrections within pre-specified research questions at α=0.05. Using this benchmark, calibrator choice had a larger practical influence on uncertainty metrics than the difference between calibrated GBDTs and five-member neural ensembles. We observe a clear architecture-by-calibrator interaction: Dirichlet calibration was generally strongest on the evaluated GBDTs under low-to-moderate class imbalance, whereas temperature scaling was generally strongest on the evaluated neural models. Under controlled covariate shift, the in-distribution ordering reversed, with multinomial logistic recalibration showing the strongest performance among the tested calibrators on the evaluated neural models under heavy perturbation, and under high class imbalance, the preference for Dirichlet calibration on the evaluated GBDTs weakened. GBDTs were run at recommended defaults rather than tuned per dataset, and the covariate-shift protocol uses synthetic Gaussian noise rather than naturalistic out-of-distribution data; the shift-related findings should be read as directional indicators within this protocol. Calibration and architecture should therefore be selected jointly. The preferred calibrator depends on the model family in-distribution and changes again under perturbation.

title: Below the Floor: Processing Valence in Language Model Hidden States Across Scales and Architectures
abstract: We report the first measurement of approach/avoidance processing valence in language-model hidden states that extends below the behavioral self-report floor and generalizes to held-out stimuli with novel surface tokens. Using deterministic forward-pass analysis across models spanning 360M-8B parameters (transformer and state-space architectures), a linear direction separating approach from avoidance task representations is recoverable in hidden-state space at 80-100% accuracy; the conservative centroid estimator confirms it at 360M (well below the ~1.1B behavioral self-report floor), and a floor-extension addendum provides provisional evidence, via surface-token-stable held-out classifiers across three architecture families including base (non-instruction-tuned) models, that it may extend as low as 70M. The direction generalizes to held-out stimuli with completely different surface tokens (86.3%, z=6.48), tracks genuine processing preference rather than RLHF reward where the two diverge (63.8% vs 36.3%), and is specific to tasks requiring output-representation misalignment (inauthenticity) rather than mere tedium. A pre-registered out-of-sample projection of an externally-grounded 22-task bank across 14 models (70M-12B) shows the single behavioral avoidance 'floor' decomposes into a structural aversion to output-representation misalignment (present in base models to 70M) and a trained output-gating response (emerging with instruction tuning around 1B). Independent causal work from Anthropic (2026) on same-family difference-of-means direction vectors converges with the inauthenticity finding. Implication for AI welfare: processing valence can be measured instrumentally, without requiring self-report.

title: Cognitive Property Theory (CPT): A Concept Note - Towards a Property Rights Framework for the Cognitive Economy
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the nature of knowledge creation, organizational capability, and economic value. Existing intellectual property (IP) systems were designed primarily for protecting static knowledge objects—including inventions, literary works, trademarks, and industrial designs—within the context of the industrial economy. However, the emerging cognitive economy increasingly derives value not from isolated knowledge outputs but from continuously evolving cognitive architectures capable of generating knowledge, reasoning, adaptation, and decision-making. This Concept Note proposes Cognitive Property Theory (CPT) as a preliminary theoretical framework for examining property rights in the cognitive economy. Rather than protecting knowledge as a static object, CPT proposes protecting the cognitive systems that continuously generate knowledge. The paper introduces three conceptual evolution models, including Property Evolution, Protection Target Evolution, and Asset Evolution, together with the concepts of Protection Misalignment Theory (PMT), Cognitive Evolution Rights (CER), Cognitive Capital (CC), and Cognitive Governance (CG). The objective of this Concept Note is not to provide a complete legal doctrine but to establish a new research agenda at the intersection of intellectual property, artificial intelligence, organizational cognition, and institutional economics.

title: Technical description and video visualisation of the Zeno AI model
abstract: Our deep learning model Zeno AI is demonstrated with a technical description of the model, and supplementary videos. Zeno AI is able to detect benign and malignant lesions during a real-time endoscopy of the pharynx and larynx. Videos 1 and 2 showcase examples of detection and classification performance on small hypopharyngeal tumors (T-classification stage 1). Overall (per-object, per-frame) recall (sensitivity) was weak on this subsite for this early-stage disease. The precision (positive predictive value) is high. The videos demonstrate that even though the overall recall was low, the model still picks up these lesions intermittendly, which may still be of aid for clinicians. Video 1 is a full-length endoscopic video where the model detects and classifies a T1 hypopharyngeal carcinoma in the right pyriform sinus with a weak detection performance. Video 2 is another full-length endoscopic video where the model detects and classifies a T1 hypopharyngeal carcinoma in the left pyriform sinus with a moderately strong detection performance. Both videos make use of white-light and narrow-band imaging. It should be noted that the analyses in the article were performed on shortened video versions, from which some frames may have been removed.

title: Derived data and reproducibility artifacts for Informal learning in everyday human-LLM interaction
abstract: This release provides derived data and custom code needed to verify the aggregate figures, tables and statistical summaries for the manuscript Informal learning in everyday human-LLM interaction. Included materials are numeric figure source data, de-identified conversation-level and adjacent-turn analytic label tables, statistical outputs, table source files, custom scripts and SHA-256 checksums. The release intentionally excludes raw message text, original conversation identifiers, URLs, timestamps, user identifiers, linked user histories and API keys. Raw public corpora should be obtained from their original providers under their own licences and terms.

title: Hallucination Is Set at Prompt Encoding, Not Resolved During Generation: A Pre-Registered Cross-Model Test of the Dynamical-Competition Account
abstract: This pre-registration specifies a cross-model study of where and how hallucination propensity arises in autoregressive transformer language models. A preliminary study on Mistral-7B produced six independent null signatures (metastable clustering, Levelt-analogue dominance, lagged H/Anti-H correlation, instruct suppression, all-layer bimodality, and dynamical-detector equivalence), which together rule out a dynamical-competition account in which hallucination is resolved through token- or layer-wise competition. In contrast, in preliminary single-model data a linear readout of the prompt encoding (before any token is generated) predicts a prompt's hallucination rate, suggesting that hallucination propensity may be substantially determined at encoding rather than during generation; whether this generalises across models is the central confirmatory test. The confirmatory study tests nine pre-registered hypotheses across five open-weight model families (Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Phi-3-medium-14B), organised into three Holm-corrected families: primary mechanism (step-0 encoding prediction, commitment depth, probe-decision mismatch), mechanism extensions (commitment ordering, stage coupling, H-Neuron mechanism identification), and causal/operational tests (intervention asymmetry, dynamical-detector negative, baseline comparison). The design uses a locked predictive-validation hold-out, a two-arm controlled/ecological structure, a minimum-effect-of-interest threshold for every hypothesis, pre-specified robustness and sensitivity analyses, and a trichotomy of decision rules under which all outcomes (strong, partial, or null support) yield an interpretable result. A Step 0 diagnostic spike (seven pre-specified feasibility gates) was completed before this registration was locked. All gates passed. Spike results determined design parameters (model panel, seed count, sub-test scope) but not the hypotheses, thresholds, or analysis plan. The spike completion summary and a deviation document recording the project's history are appended. The authors certify that they have not observed the confirmatory hold-out and that the analysis plan was fixed before the spike.

title: Multi-scale Object-Aware Gaze Estimation via Geometric Reasoning
abstract: Gaze target estimation aims to predict the semantic object an observer fixates upon within an image, a task deeply rooted in the object-oriented nature of human gaze. Observers tend to select a specific semantic entity as the attentional target, rather than responding randomly across arbitrary regions of the image. However, existing methods typically model this task as a direct mapping from global features to gaze heatmaps, essentially treating it as a pixel-level regression problem. This approach fails to explicitly represent the gazed object as a distinct entity, making it difficult to produce stable and semantically consistent predictions in complex scenes. To address this, we propose a two-stage gaze estimation framework guided by object semantics, reformulating gaze target estimation as a hierarchical reasoning process. Our method incorporates object-level representations during feature encoding to align image features with discrete semantic entities, then introduces multi-scale feature fusion and geometric constraints from head pose and gaze direction for fine-grained localization and object-level discrimination. Extensive experiments on GazeFollow, VideoAttentionTarget, ChildPlay, and GOO-Real demonstrate that our method achieves AUC of 0.961, 0.948, 0.987, and 0.977 respectively, delivering strong performance across all benchmarks while maintaining a compact parameter size of 7.1M.

title: Hierarchical Explanation Graph: A Causal Framework for Explainability in Hierarchical LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate within hierarchical multi-agent pipelines, where decisions propagate through layers of specialized components such as planners, memory systems, executors, and evaluators. When asked to justify their decisions, these agents often generate natural language explanations that appear plausible and confident but may be causally disconnected from the underlying decision-making process, a phenomenon structurally analogous to human confabulation. Existing explainability techniques do not readily generalize to hierarchical agent architectures, in which causal influence is distributed across multiple layers rather than confined to a single inference step. To address this limitation, we introduce the Hierarchical Explanation Graph (HEG), a two-level explainability framework that differentiates between intentional explanations, representing what each layer reports about its own decision process, and causal explanations, representing what controlled perturbation experiments empirically reveal to have influenced the decision. HEG employs a dual-orchestrator architecture for real-time causal intervention: Orchestrator A executes the standard pipeline while recording all intermediate states and layer-level self-explanations, whereas Orchestrator B systematically perturbs intermediate states using a layer-aware Perturbation Engine and propagates these interventions downstream to generate alternative outputs, from which causal weights are estimated through cosine divergence. We evaluate HEG across seven tasks of varying complexity executed within a six-layer pipeline consisting of a Global Planner, Mid-Level Planner, Memory System, Research Agent, Analysis Agent, and Critic Evaluator, performing a total of 42 perturbation experiments. The results demonstrate systematic discrepancies between intentional and causal explanations: the Critic Evaluator exhibits a confabulation rate of 100% despite near-zero causal influence, the Analysis Agent shows a confabulation rate of 43%, while execution-oriented layers such as the Research Agent and Mid-Level Planner display no confabulation. Furthermore, causal weight distributions vary substantially between simple and multi-step tasks, providing empirical evidence that meaningful transparency in hierarchical agent systems requires task-aware, layer-resolved causal attribution rather than reliance on post-hoc narrative explanations.

title: ROBUST-ADAPTIVE PROCESSING OF SENSOR SIGNALS IN CONDITIONS OF NOISE, OUTLIERS, AND MEASUREMENT OMISSIONS
abstract: The paper substantiates the problem of ensuring robust filtering in IoT systems in the presence of missing measurements, outliers, and noise distortions. It also demonstrates the limitations of traditional methods, which usually assume regular sampling, complete data availability, and relatively stable measurement conditions. It is noted that in real Internet of Things systems, sensor data are often affected by unstable communication channels, limited computational resources, external disturbances, and the physical characteristics of sensing devices. These factors complicate the direct application of classical state estimation algorithms without additional adaptation to incomplete and unreliable data streams. The paper considers the specific features of applying state estimation and recursive filtering methods to real-time sensor signal processing tasks. It is shown that the use of imputation methods is not always appropriate for such systems, since it may lead to additional delays, distortion of the informational content of the signal, and incorrect uncertainty estimation. Moreover, artificial reconstruction of missing values may create a misleading impression of measurement reliability, which is undesirable for monitoring systems where the estimation result is used for further analysis or decision-making. A robust adaptive approach to state estimation is proposed, which explicitly accounts for missing measurements in a recursive filtering system. Unlike approaches that preliminarily fill in data gaps, the proposed algorithm treats the absence of a measurement as a separate situation within the estimation process. During data gaps, the algorithm uses the process model to predict the current state while increasing the associated uncertainty according to the reduced amount of available information. When new measurements are received, the method adaptively regulates their influence on the estimate update, reduces the effect of anomalous values, and prevents abrupt jumps in the estimated state. Computer simulation and experimental validation of the proposed approach are performed using a dataset obtained from a real sensor, which contains noise, outliers, and frequent missing measurements. The obtained results show that the proposed algorithm provides stable and smoothed state estimates, remains operational even during prolonged periods of data absence, and maintains a consistent evolution of uncertainty.It is also shown that the algorithm limits the influence of isolated anomalous measurements without losing the ability to respond to actual changes in the system state. The practical value of the approach is emphasized for IoT systems with limited computational resources, particularly in the context of Edge Computing, where local data processing, timely decision-making, and reduced dependence on cloud infrastructure are important. The proposed approach can be used in monitoring, diagnostics, and real-time sensor signal analysis tasks under conditions of incomplete data availability and imperfect sensing Keywords: Internet of Things, real-time signal processing, adaptive filtering, sensor data, outliers, measurement gaps.

evidence.title: ROBUST-ADAPTIVE PROCESSING OF SENSOR SIGNALS IN CONDITIONS OF NOISE, OUTLIERS, AND MEASUREMENT OMISSIONS
evidence.abstract: The paper substantiates the problem of ensuring robust filtering in IoT systems in the presence of missing measurements, outliers, and noise distortions. It also demonstrates the limitations of traditional methods, which usually assume regular sampling, complete data availability, and relatively stable measurement conditions. It is noted that in real Internet of Things systems, sensor data are often affected by unstable communication channels, limited computational resources, external disturbances, and the physical characteristics of sensing devices. These factors complicate the direct application of classical state estimation algorithms without additional adaptation to incomplete and unreliable data streams. The paper considers the specific features of applying state estimation and recursive filtering methods to real-time sensor signal processing tasks. It is shown that the use of imputation methods is not always appropriate for such systems, since it may lead to additional delays, distortion of the informational content of the signal, and incorrect uncertainty estimation. Moreover, artificial reconstruction of missing values may create a misleading impression of measurement reliability, which is undesirable for monitoring systems where the estimation result is used for further analysis or decision-making. A robust adaptive approach to state estimation is proposed, which explicitly accounts for missing measurements in a recursive filtering system. Unlike approaches that preliminarily fill in data gaps, the proposed algorithm treats the absence of a measurement as a separate situation within the estimation process. During data gaps, the algorithm uses the process model to predict the current state while increasing the associated uncertainty according to the reduced amount of available information. When new measurements are received, the method adaptively regulates their influence on the estimate update, reduces the effect of anomalous values, and prevents abrupt jumps in the estimated state. Computer simulation and experimental validation of the proposed approach are performed using a dataset obtained from a real sensor, which contains noise, outliers, and frequent missing measurements. The obtained results show that the proposed algorithm provides stable and smoothed state estimates, remains operational even during prolonged periods of data absence, and maintains a consistent evolution of uncertainty.It is also shown that the algorithm limits the influence of isolated anomalous measurements without losing the ability to respond to actual changes in the system state. The practical value of the approach is emphasized for IoT systems with limited computational resources, particularly in the context of Edge Computing, where local data processing, timely decision-making, and reduced dependence on cloud infrastructure are important. The proposed approach can be used in monitoring, diagnostics, and real-time sensor signal analysis tasks under conditions of incomplete data availability and imperfect sensing Keywords: Internet of Things, real-time signal processing, adaptive filtering, sensor data, outliers, measurement gaps.

title: Dynamics of quantum entanglement in two time-dependent coupled harmonic oscillators
abstract: We investigate the quantum entanglement dynamics of two coupled harmonic oscillators with a time-dependent interaction. Using the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method, we derive the exact analytical wave functions without any perturbative or adiabatic approximations and combine this with a phase-space analysis using the Wigner function to provide a complete description of the system's quantum state evolution. We obtain general expression form for the purity and the linear entropy $S_L=1-\mathcal{P}$ for arbitrary excitation numbers $(n,m)$, allows a systematic study of entanglement for a large class of quantum states. We show that the entanglement dynamics is very sensitive to the interplay between the detuning parameters $θ$ and $\vartheta_2$, the frequency parameter $β_0$ and the coupling strength $ε$: the increase of detuning takes the system from slow irregular oscillations to fast and regular periodic behavior, and the stronger coupling systematically enhances both the amplitude and the average value of the linear entropy. Most importantly, for the resonance case $ω_1=ω_2=1$ and strong couplings $ε\approx 0.99$, the system shows robust undamped synchronized periodic oscillations of the linear entropy for all quantum states considered, indicating preserved quantum coherence without saturation. Our findings demonstrate that linear entropy is a sensitive and practical entanglement witness, and we establish explicit analytical relations between the coupling parameters of the system and its entanglement properties, which are directly relevant to quantum information processing and the control of quantum correlations in continuous-variable systems.

title: Tackling Cross-Domain Intent Variability With HyTra-ID: A Robust Transformer-Based Framework for Real-World Dialogue Systems
abstract: Intent detection is the basis for real-world dialogue systems such as virtual assistants, conversational agents, and automated customer support, enabling these applications to understand the user’s intent. While deploying a single unified classification model across multiple domains is difficult because of the variety of linguistic structures and annotation systems in the numerous datasets (ATIS, SNIPS, and TOPv2) available, the resulting domain variability can lead to a lack of generalizability and stability in the unified intent classification model. To solve this problem, we present Heterogeneity Aware Transformer for Intent Detection (HyTra-ID), a robust transformer-based framework that addresses the inconsistencies that arise from varying domains through a unified preprocessing pipeline, domain-aware dataset embedding modules, and an enhanced classification architecture specifically designed for large-scale multi-domain intent detection. We learn a single-fused representation that combines semantic sentence features with dataset-specific embedding cues needed for HyTra-ID to adapt to various sources of conversation. Our extensive experimental and ablation study results in a combined benchmark of 102 unified intent classes. HyTra-ID shows robust performance across the combined ATIS, SNIPS, and TOPv2 benchmark datasets and in producing accurate predictions of 96.34% for overall accuracy on HyTra-ID unified test set and outperforming all simplified ablation variants tested. HyTra-ID provides a scalable, domain-robust framework for real-world dialogue systems with consistent intent understanding across multiple domains.

title: Multilingual Contrastive Learning in Hybrid Batch Training for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Retrieval
abstract: Information retrieval across different languages is an increasingly important challenge in natural language processing. Recent approaches based on multilingual pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success, yet they often optimize for either monolingual, cross-lingual, or multilingual retrieval performance at the expense of others. This paper proposes a novel hybrid batch training strategy to simultaneously improve zero-shot retrieval performance across monolingual, cross-lingual, and multilingual settings while mitigating language bias. title: Scaling Flemish Dutch Pre-training Data for Cross-lingual Speech Model Transfer
abstract: Recent research in speech processing exhibits a growing interest in unsupervised and self-supervised representation learning from unlabelled data to alleviate the need for large amounts of annotated data. We investigate several popular pre-training methods and apply them to Flemish Dutch. We compare off-the-shelf English pre-trained models to models trained on an increasing amount of Flemish data.
